blocks.html: In Hebrew, the phrase “I am” ( א ֶֽהְי ֶ֖ה , ehyeh), is linguistically related to Elohim’s name, יהוה (YHUH/YHVH/YHWH, often represented in English as Yahuah, Yahweh or Jehovah). Many Hebrew scholars suggest that יהוה means something like “the one who is.” In fact, the Septuagint (ancient Greek translations of the Tanakh/OT, widely used by early Jews and Christians) did not translate the second א ֶֽהְי ֶ֖ה in Shemoth/Exodus 3:14 as ἐγώ εἰμι, but rather as ὁ ὢν, “the one who is.”

Many Hebrew scholars suggest that יהוה means something like “the one who is.” In fact, the Septuagint (ancient Greek translations of the Tanakh/OT, widely used by early Jews and Christians) did not translate the second א ֶֽהְי ֶ֖ה in Shemoth/Exodus 3:14 as ἐγώ εἰμι, but rather as ὁ ὢν, “the one who is.”

blocks.html: The Hebrew word “I am” (א ֶֽהְי ֶ֖ה , ehyeh), however, is not a code word or a technical title for Elohim. It is often used by Elohim in the Tanakh/Old Testament, but rarely as His title. It is used by many people simply to refer to themselves. Yephthah (Shophtim/Judg es11:9, Ruth 2:13, Shemu’el Aleph/1 Sam 18:18, Jonathan, Shemu’el Aleph/1 Sam 23:17), Shemu’el Bet/2 Sam 16:18, Iyob/Job 12:4) and many others use it to refer to themselves. It is a quite normal way to say “I am” for anyone.

blocks.html: In the Brit Chadashah/New Testament, ἐγώ εἰμι is used by Yahushua, Yudas (Matt 26:25), Gabriel (Luqas 1:19), the blind man (Yochanan/John 9:9), Kepha/Peter (Ma’asei/Acts 10:21) and Sha’ul/Paul (Ma’’asei/Acts 22:3, 26:29, Rom. 11:13, Timotiyos Aleph/1 Tim 1:15), always to refer to themselves. This matches the use in Greek outside the BC/NT. The Septuagint uses “I am” (ἐγώ εἰμι) in very normal ways. Elohim uses the phrase often, but so does Ya’’aqov/Jacob (Bereshit/Genesis27:32), Deborah (Shophtim/Judges 5:3), Gideon (Shophtim/Judges 6:15) and others. As I have searched through other works written in ancient Greek (Philo, the Pseudepigrapha, Plato and other philosophers), I have run across many such ordinary occurrences of ἐγώ εἰμι.

By this we know the spirit of truth (Yahushua was not יהוה incarnate) and the spirit of error (the doctrine of incarnation).
